(a)      The  minority  of  candidates  scored  any  marks  in  this  question.  Candidates  must  be  taught  to  study
                  the  basic  shapes  of  the  exponential  and  logarithmic  graphs,  as  well  as  their  transformations.  Most
                  candidates  tried  to  use  the  table  function  in  the  calculator  and  ended  up  with  a  shape  that  is  not  a
                  smooth descending exponential curve, with the x-axis as asymptote. It should also be noted that the
                  time starts at t = 0. The descending curve must only be in the first quadrant.

         (b)      It was occasionally seen that candidates just tried out different numbers (“trial and error method”) and
                  then concluded to a number of weeks. It is not an acceptable method for Advanced Subsidiary Level.
                  It was expected of candidates to be able to deal with the appropriate algebra. The question asked for
                  the  number  of  complete  weeks. The  expectation  was  to  first  see  the  decimal  version  of  exactly  the
                  half of 5000, followed by a conclusion.

(a)      Well    answered.    Some    candidates    only    used    the    remainder    theorem    to    show    that    the    remainder    is
                  –    5    and    never    calculated    the    quotient.   This    resulted    in    the    loss    of    marks.   Teachers    are    advised    to
                  teach   synthetic   division   as   well.   It   is   a   faster   method   than   long   division   and   the   chances   of   making
                  mistakes are less.

         (b)      Moderately  answered.  Very  few  candidates  realised  that  the  question  was  structured  to  show  them
                  that     (x     +     2)     is     a     factor     of     p(x).     Most     candidates     used     long     division     again,     ignoring     the     instruction
                  of    “hence”,    which    means    the    answer    of    the   part (a)    must    be    used    to    answer    this    question.        Many
                  candidates solved the cubic equation, instead of factorising.

                  It should be noted that 6x2 – 19x + 15 cannot be factorised as                                                                                        . It must be written
                  as (3x – 5)(2x – 3).
                  It was also seen that some candidates used calculators that could solve cubic equations. They only
                  wrote down three brackets without any working, which resulted in the loss of all the marks.

         (c)      Moderately  answered.  Some  candidates  could  not  have  been  familiar  with  the  word  roots. They  did
                  not realise that they just needed to solve an equation equal to zero. Many candidates did not realise
                  that all three brackets in part (b) had to be solved. It was often seen that candidates wrongly equated
                  each bracket to 5. Other candidates misunderstood the question and tried to comment on the nature
                  of the roots.

(a)    This very easy question, was surprisingly poorly answered by many candidates. It seemed as if some
              centres     did     not     teach     the     trapezium-rule     at     all.     Candidates     clearly     did     not     know     how     to     apply     the
              quoted equation in the formula sheet.
              Many candidates lost their accuracy mark, due to premature rounding in the question. Candidates
              wans to make use of a table, it is advised that they use ln 1, ln 3, ln 5 etc and not the decimal
              equivalent. If decimals are used, it must be used to at least 4 decimal places not to lose the
              accuracy of the final answer.

       (b)    Extremely poorly answered. Very few candidates realised (x2 – 4          x + 4) = (x – 2)2. Candidates who got
              the  squared  bracket,  failed  to  apply  the  log-laws  to  rewrite  the  3  ln(x2 – 4          x  +  4)  to  6  ln(x  –  2)  before
              the answer to part (a)  could  be  used.  Common  wrong  working  seen  was  (11.5)                                                                                                                                                            2,  where  candidates
              interpreted the square as squaring the answer to part (a).

       (c)    Moderately answered. Candidates should be taught the basic shapes of log- and exponential graphs,
              as well as their transformations. Tables should NOT be used     to     draw     graphs     at     this     level.     Most
              candidates failed to indicate the asymptote at the correct place. It was often seen that the graph was
              only   drawn   in   the  first  quadrant,  instead   of  in   both   the  first  and  fourth  quadrants.   Very  poor   shapes
              were seen. It should be a clear ascending graph that is not flattening off as the x-values increased.
              It was occasionally seen that candidates could not distinguish between the exponential- and the
              log-graphs. If both graphs were sketch, without labels, it resulted in the loss of all marks for the
              question.

       (d)    Poorly  answered.  Since  English  is  not  the  mother  tongue  of  most  candidates,  teachers  should  take
              care to teach explanations in the easiest possible way. It is not advisable to refer to convex of concave,
              as candidates get confused with the concepts very easily. It is not acceptable to refer to a graph as
              sloping    up    (ascending)    or    sloping    down    (descending)    as    a    reason.       The    easiest    description    in    this
              case was to refer to the edges of the trapeziums being below the curve. Reference must be made to
              both the curve, as well as the trapezium.

             skills.   It   was   often   seem   that   –   4   sin   2x   was   wrongly   integrated   as   –   2   cos   2x,   instead   of   2   cos   2x.
             Cos   x was also often wrongly integrated to – sin           x. Another  common  mistake  was  to  integrate  1  as
             well. These candidates did not realise that they needed to apply the boundaries to the integrant first
             and the result must be equalled to 1. Many candidates failed to apply the bottom boundary (0). They
             presumed it is 0, not realising that cos 0 = 1.

             It is not enough to only find a positive and negative value. Both values must be seen and the candidates
             must conclude                                                                                    that there is a change in sign. Some candidates just substituted 1.3 and 1.6 and concluded
             that it is a change of sign, without calculating thevalues.
